cim_eredeti: FDA Artificial Intelligence & AI/ML Device Rules
szoveg_eredeti:
Written and maintained by CASRAI Editorial Board

FDA artificial intelligence regulation governs how artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) algorithms used in healthcare—whether deployed as standalone Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) or embedded as Software in a Medical Device (SiMD)—are classified, validated, cleared or approved for marketing, and monitored post-market in the United States. Coordinated by the Center for Devices and Radiological Health (FDA CDRH) and its Digital Health Center of Excellence (DHCoE) alongside CDER and CBER AI regulatory frameworks, the agency regulates clinical AI through risk-based premarket pathways, Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP) principles, and statutory Clinical Decision Support (CDS) boundaries.

Before selecting a premarket submission pathway, developers and clinical investigators must first determine whether an AI algorithm meets the statutory definition of a medical device under Section 201(h) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic (FD&C) Act, or whether it qualifies as Non-Device Clinical Decision Support (CDS) under Section 520(o)(1)(E) (enacted by Section 3060 of the 21st Century Cures Act).

Under the FDA’s final guidance on Clinical Decision Support Software (September 2022), a clinical software function is excluded from FDA device regulation only if it satisfies all four statutory criteria simultaneously:

Any AI/ML model that analyzes medical images or physiological waveforms (failing Criterion 1), targets patients directly rather than HCPs (failing Criterion 3), or operates as an unexplainable “black-box” urgency triage score without transparent clinical logic (failing Criterion 4) is regulated as an AI/ML-enabled medical device (AIaMD).

Note that the FDA does not “certify” AI algorithms (why FDA does not certify devices); instead, the agency clears Class II devices via 510(k), grants marketing authorization via De Novo, or approves Class III devices via PMA.

Submissions for 510(k), De Novo, and PMA AI/ML devices are prepared and transmitted electronically using the FDA eSTAR structured submission template and must include premarket cybersecurity documentation under Section 524B (including a Software Bill of Materials and adversarial ML threat modeling).
